title: OpenAI Releases GPT-6 Cyber for Vetted Security Teams
content:
OpenAI has released GPT-6 Cyber, a cybersecurity model for approved security teams that can help find and test software flaws and develop fixes, with access limited to users who have been checked.
OpenAI says the model is available to select customers in its Daybreak Red program, which supports advanced, approved security work. OpenAI plans to expand access to other approved customers. OpenAI says the model found 81 previously unknown, severe vulnerabilities in Firefox.
It helped develop possible fixes. Mozilla has released fixes for many of them. For Linux, OpenAI reports that the model developed ways to take advantage of 948 flaws in the Linux kernel, the core software of the operating system.
OpenAI also reports that it disclosed 304 critical issues to Linux maintainers, along with suggested fixes. The company says the model followed the limits researchers had approved in 99.93% of tests when it was not given an instruction to deploy it. OpenAI says the model followed those limits in every test when it was given that instruction.
OpenAI gave the model a “Critical” cybersecurity capability rating under its safety framework. The company cited the model’s ability to find and take advantage of flaws. Access controls include identity checks and security requirements for organizations.
The limited rollout reflects the risk that powerful tools for researching software flaws could be misused.

report.summary: OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber, a vetted-access security model that found 81 Firefox vulnerabilities and 948 Linux kernel exploits, earning a Critical capability rating.
report.background: GPT-6 Cyber arrives as AI models move from code completion into autonomous vulnerability discovery, a dual-use capability that can strengthen defenders or accelerate attackers. Security teams already use fuzzing, static analysis, and bounty programs, but frontier models can chain reasoning across codebases and generate exploit hypotheses. OpenAI's Daybreak Red program is a gated-access effort for approved security work, reflecting growing concern among labs and governments about misuse. The release also tests responsible-disclosure norms: model-found bugs must be reported privately, fixed by maintainers, and only then discussed publicly. Mozilla and Linux kernel maintainers are early test cases for how AI-assisted security research scales.
key_points: Access is restricted to vetted customers in OpenAI's Daybreak Red program, with identity checks and organizational security requirements. OpenAI says it plans to widen access to other approved customers, but the gated rollout signals that the model is treated as sensitive dual-use infrastructure rather than a general-purpose chatbot.

OpenAI says GPT-6 Cyber found 81 previously unknown severe vulnerabilities in Firefox and helped develop candidate fixes. Mozilla has released fixes for many of them, making this one of the largest public examples of an AI model contributing to real-world browser security patches.

For the Linux kernel, OpenAI reports the model generated ways to exploit 948 flaws and disclosed 304 critical issues to maintainers with suggested fixes. The scale illustrates how AI can compress vulnerability research timelines, though maintainers still must validate, patch, and coordinate disclosure.

OpenAI claims the model respected researcher-approved limits in 99.93% of tests without a deployment instruction, and in every test when given one. Those figures are self-reported, but they matter because autonomous security agents need reliable guardrails before broader release.

Under OpenAI's safety framework, GPT-6 Cyber received a "Critical" cybersecurity capability rating due to its ability to find and exploit flaws. That rating explains the access controls and likely shapes how regulators and enterprises evaluate frontier-model risk.
report.impact: The release signals that frontier AI is becoming a practical security-research tool, not just a coding assistant. For the AI industry, it raises the bar for capability evaluations and gated deployment. Security teams gain a faster way to triage code and generate exploit hypotheses, but they must verify outputs and manage disclosure. Developers should expect shorter patch windows and more AI-generated bug reports, while maintainers may face reporting volume. Regular users benefit if fixes land faster, but also face risk if similar models leak or are misused. The bigger test is whether gated access, identity checks, and disclosure norms can keep dual-use capability out of the wrong hands without slowing defenders.
report.tools: Watch OpenAI's Daybreak Red access program, Mozilla security advisories, and Linux kernel CVE/disclosure channels. For hands-on work, explore OSS-Fuzz and ClusterFuzz for fuzzing, CodeQL and Semgrep for static analysis, AFL++ and syzkaller for kernel/binary testing, and OSV, GitHub Advisory Database, and OpenSSF Scorecard for vulnerability and dependency tracking. These open tools complement, rather than replace, model-assisted vulnerability research.
